blocks.markdown: The foreign currency deposit system

This lesson covers RA 6426: who may keep foreign currency deposits and where, what banks may do with them, the absolute confidentiality of Section 8, the express bar on attachment and garnishment with its narrow Salvacion exception, and how this regime relates to RA 1405. If the first two lessons taught 'secret with exits,' this one teaches 'secret with almost no exits.'

RA 6426, approved April 4, 1972, created a second deposit universe inside Philippine banks: accounts denominated in foreign currency, fenced by their own confidentiality, withdrawability, and tax rules. Whenever a question involves dollar (or other foreign currency) deposits, reach for RA 6426 first — RA 1405 is the wrong statute unless a later law expressly bridges the two.

Three coverage notes. **Who:** any natural or juridical person — individuals and companies, residents and non-residents alike. **Where:** only with Philippine banks in good standing that the Central Bank (now BSP) has designated for the purpose. **What currency:** foreign currencies acceptable as part of the international reserve, minus any the BSP requires surrendered under the old Central Bank Act framework. Example: an exporter keeping dollar receipts or an OFW family holding dollar savings both sit squarely inside this section.

Five bank powers, two student takeaways. **Numbered accounts** are expressly allowed — secrecy engineered into the account structure itself. And the deposit can be **used as loan collateral** or evidenced by **discountable certificates**, which shows FCDs are working commercial instruments, not museum pieces. None of these powers lets outsiders pry: dealing with one's own deposit (collateral, certificates) is the depositor's choice, not an exception for third parties.

The depositor's freedom side of the bargain: withdraw anytime, move the money abroad freely — the State adds no restriction beyond what the bank contract itself says. This is why FCDs attracted inflows alongside confidentiality and tax exemption. But freedom for the depositor is not freedom for outsiders: creditors, investigators, and courts hitting Section 8 find the door shut.
Section 8: absolute confidentiality

Compare this with RA 1405 word by word. **One exit only:** the depositor's written permission — no impeachment, no bribery/dereliction court order, no subject-matter exception. **A wider wall:** 'in no instance' examined or inquired into by any person, official, bureau, or office, whether judicial, administrative, legislative, or any other entity public or private. **Plus a process shield:** exempt from attachment, garnishment, or any other order or process of any court, legislature, agency, or administrative body whatsoever. Coverage spans RA 6426/PD 1035 deposits and PD 1034 offshore-banking deposits alike.

Section 8 was not always absolute, and the history is examinable. **1972 (original):** FCD secrecy simply followed RA 1405 — so all four RA 1405 exceptions applied. **1976 (PD 1035):** kept RA 1405 governance and added that usury and uniform-currency laws do not apply to FCD transactions. **1977 (PD 1246):** imposed the current absolute regime to accelerate foreign currency inflows, pairing it with full tax exemption and vested-rights protection. PD 1034, cited in the coverage clause, is the decree that authorized the offshore banking system — so offshore-banking-unit deposits share the shield.

Application drill: a subpoena in a plunder case that validly opens a peso account under Ejercito cannot open a dollar account under Section 8's own terms — there is no bribery exception to invoke. An impeachment court, a civil litigant tracing 'subject matter' funds, and a sheriff with a writ of execution all hit the same wall. The only Section 8 key is the depositor's written permission. Later 'notwithstanding RA 6426' statutes (AMLA, tax, PDIC charter) are separate doors with their own procedures — they do not rewrite Section 8 itself.

Context for the incentive package, not a secrecy rule itself: eligible FCDs plus all their interest and earnings are fully tax-exempt either way — resident or not, in business or not. The original 1972 version exempted only non-resident interest; PD 1246 made it blanket. On a secrecy exam this section answers 'why is the system so protective' rather than 'who may look.'

FCDs are PDIC-insured under RA 3591 like peso deposits — with one currency twist: payout comes in the same currency the deposit is denominated in. So a dollar depositor of a failed bank is paid in dollars (subject to coverage limits and PDIC procedure, which the PDIC module teaches). Secrecy during the bank's life and insurance after its death are companion protections, not contradictions.

Later rights-decreasing laws apply only to deposits made AFTER them; existing deposits keep their old rights. (Section 7 says the same for Central Bank regulations.) Honest flag for advanced answers: this protection sits in tension with later 'notwithstanding RA 6426' inquiry statutes — AMLA Sec. 11, NIRC Sec. 6(F), PDIC Charter Sec. 8 — whose express override is standardly taught as reaching FCDs through their own procedures. No Supreme Court decision squarely applies Sec. 12-A to block those statutes, so state both texts and mark the interplay unsettled rather than pretending it is resolved.

Two differences from RA 1405's penalty: the violation must be **willful**, and the ranges have **floors and ceilings** — one to five years, P5,000 to P25,000, or both. The penalty covers violations of the Act and of Monetary Board regulations issued under it, so unlawful disclosure of FCD information and breach of FCD operating rules share one punishment clause.
The garnishment rule

Run every garnishment question as a pair. **Peso deposit + final judgment:** garnishable — Ortega says execution is not inquiry and disclosure is incidental. **Foreign currency deposit + final judgment:** exempt — Sec. 8 says so expressly, and Salvacion refused to apply the exemption only because letting a transient wrongdoer hide dollars from his child victim would make the law an instrument of injustice. If the facts lack Salvacion's extreme equities, the exemption holds. Never cite Salvacion as permission to garnish FCDs generally.

blocks.markdown: The relationship in one paragraph: RA 6426 began as RA 1405's junior partner (original Sec. 8 pointed FCD secrecy to RA 1405), then PD 1246 made it the stricter standalone regime — fewer exits, plus immunity from legal process. Later 'notwithstanding' statutes bridge both worlds: AMLA Sec. 11, NIRC Sec. 6(F), and PDIC Charter Sec. 8 each expressly override RA 1405 AND RA 6426 through their own procedures. The unclaimed-balances law and Ortega garnishment, by contrast, operate in peso-deposit territory. State Sec. 12-A's vested-rights rule whenever those bridges come up, and flag its interplay as the module's one genuinely unsettled point.

Remember: FCD answers have a fixed shape — (1) identify the deposit as foreign currency under RA 6426; (2) state the Sec. 8 rule (written permission only; no attachment/garnishment); (3) test Salvacion's equities before ever excepting; (4) check 'notwithstanding' bridges with their procedures; (5) close with Sec. 12-A prospectivity where later laws are involved.
